html:
The big picture

Every robot has an electrical system: a power source feeds sensors, a processing unit and actuators. To reason about it you need four quantities — charge Q, voltage V (energy per charge), current I (charge per time) and power P = VI — and one material property, resistance, linked to them by Ohm's law V = IR. Two conservation laws then solve any DC circuit: Kirchhoff's voltage law (around a loop, the rises equal the drops — energy is conserved) and Kirchhoff's current law (what flows into a node flows out — charge is conserved). Resistors in series add; in parallel their conductances add. Real circuits are simplified step by step into series and parallel groups, and circuits with several sources are solved one source at a time with superposition.

Robot electrical system

Charge, current and voltage

Charge

  • Unit: coulombs (C).
  • Like charges repel, unlike charges attract.
  • A neutral body contains equal amounts of positive and negative charge.

Voltage

  • Separating charges (body A with an excess of positive charge, body B with an excess of negative charge) takes work. Moving a charge Q from one to the other against the attraction takes energy W:
V = \frac{W}{Q}
Symbols
  • V — voltage (V, volt = J/C) — this course writes V; the physics prep course wrote U for the same quantity
  • W — work (energy) needed to move the charge from one body to the other (J)
  • Q — the charge moved (C, coulomb)

Current

  • Connect A and B with a conductor and charge flows; the rate of flow is the current:
I = \frac{Q}{t}
Symbols
  • I — current (A, ampere = C/s)
  • Q — charge that flows past a point (C)
  • t — the time it takes (s)
  • The electrons move from B (negative) to A (positive); the arrow for current points the other way, from A to B (conventional current). Put a lamp in the path and the flowing charge does work in it.
Intuition

Voltage is like the height difference in a water system, current like the flow rate, a resistor like a narrow pipe. A big height difference with no pipe gives no flow (a battery on the shelf: voltage, no current); a wide pipe with a small drop gives a large flow. Voltage is always between two points — that's why the slides draw two bodies, A and B.

Common mistake

"Current flows the way the electrons go." By convention, current points from + to - outside the source — the direction positive charges would move. Electrons in a metal wire drift the opposite way. Circuit analysis always uses conventional current; the result is the same, only the sign bookkeeping must be consistent.

Power

Power is the rate of energy usage:

P = \frac{W}{t}, \qquad V = \frac{W}{Q} \;\Rightarrow\; W = VQ, \qquad P = \frac{VQ}{t}, \qquad I = \frac{Q}{t} \;\Rightarrow\; P = VI
Symbols
  • P — power: energy used per second (W = J/s)
  • W — energy/work (J); t — time (s)
  • V — voltage (V); Q — charge (C); I — current (A)

Examples

  • During a half-second interval, a certain battery delivers a charge of three coulombs. Determine the resulting current.
  • A device delivers a current of 25 mA. Determine the charge transferred in two seconds, along with the equivalent total number of electrons. The charge of an electron is -1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}.
  • 100 joules are expended to move a 20 coulomb charge from point A to point B. Determine the resulting voltage.
  • If a 9-volt battery delivers a current of 0.1 amps, determine the power delivered in watts.
Worked example — the four slide 10 examples, picking the right definition
  1. Charge and time given → current: I = \frac{Q}{t} = \frac{3\,\mathrm{C}}{0.5\,\mathrm{s}} = 6\,\mathrm{A}.
  2. Current and time given → charge: Q = I t = 0.025\,\mathrm{A} \cdot 2\,\mathrm{s} = 0.05\,\mathrm{C}. Charge → number of electrons: \frac{0.05}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 3.12 \times 10^{17} electrons.
  3. Energy and charge given → voltage: V = \frac{W}{Q} = \frac{100\,\mathrm{J}}{20\,\mathrm{C}} = 5\,\mathrm{V}.
  4. Voltage and current given → power: P = VI = 9\,\mathrm{V} \cdot 0.1\,\mathrm{A} = 0.9\,\mathrm{W}.

Units are the check: \mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C/s}, \mathrm{V} = \mathrm{J/C}, \mathrm{W} = \mathrm{J/s} = \mathrm{V \cdot A}.

Voltage sources

  • Ideal voltage sources provide a constant-amplitude voltage across their terminals.
  • The current drawn from the voltage source depends on the external load connected across it.
  • Real voltage sources have a limit on the maximum current that can be drawn from them.
  • Symbols: a circle with +/- (DC source), a battery (one cell or several), a circle with a sine wave (AC source).

Current sources

  • Ideal current sources provide a constant-amplitude current.
  • The voltage developed across the source depends on the external load connected.
  • Real current sources have a limit on the maximum voltage that can be developed across them.
  • Symbol: a circle with an arrow (the direction of the current); with a sine wave for AC.
Why may you never open-circuit a current source or short-circuit a voltage source?

An ideal voltage source insists on its voltage whatever happens: short its terminals (R = 0) and Ohm's law asks for I = V/0 — an infinite current. A real battery delivers its maximum current and heats up or burns. A current source insists on its current: leave its terminals open (R \to \infty) and it would need an infinite voltage V = IR to push the current through. The "real source" limits on the slides are exactly where these ideal promises break.

Conductance and resistance

R = \frac{1}{G} \;\text{ or }\; G = \frac{1}{R}, \qquad R = \frac{V}{I} \;\text{ or }\; V = IR \;\text{ (Ohm's law)}, \qquad R = \frac{\rho\,l}{A}
Symbols
  • R — resistance (Ω); G — conductance, how easily current flows (S, siemens = 1/Ω)
  • V — voltage across the component (V); I — current through it (A)
  • \rho — resistivity of the material (Ω·m; the table below uses Ω·cm)
  • l — length of the conductor along the current (m); A — its cross-sectional area (m²)
  • The unit of resistance is the ohm (\Omega).
  • The unit of conductance is the siemens (S).
  • For a block of material, l is the length along the current, A = w \cdot h the cross-section, \rho the resistivity of the material.
  • Ohm's law as a graph: I against V is a straight line through the origin; a steeper line means a smaller resistance.
MaterialResistivity \rho (\Omega\cdot\mathrm{cm}) at 20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}
Silver1.59 \times 10^{-6}
Copper1.68 \times 10^{-6}
Gold2.44 \times 10^{-6}
Why does resistance grow with length and shrink with cross-section?

A longer wire is like several shorter wires one after another — each piece adds its own obstacle, so R \propto l (series resistors add, see below). A thicker wire is like several thin wires side by side — more parallel paths for the charge, so R \propto 1/A (parallel conductances add). \rho is what's left: how strongly the material itself resists. That is also why the slides derive the series and parallel rules from R = \rho l / A.

Resistors

  • Resistors are available in standardised ohmic values and power ratings.
  • Along with their resistance value, resistors have a specified tolerance.
  • Example: a 220\,\Omega resistor with a tolerance of 10 % — the actual value of any given specimen from a box may be off the nameplate (nominal) value by 10 %, i.e. by 22\,\Omega (so anywhere from 198\,\Omega to 242\,\Omega).

Simple electrical circuit

A lamp, a switch and a battery: the resistance of the bulb is 36\,\Omega, the battery voltage is 9 V. What is the power consumption of the bulb?

Examples

  • A 9-volt battery is used in series to power a 40\,\Omega resistor. Determine the circulating current.
  • Determine the voltage developed across the resistor in the circuit: a 10 mA current source drives a 2.2\,\mathrm{k}\Omega resistor.
Worked example — the bulb and the two one-resistor circuits
  1. Bulb: combine P = VI with I = V/R: P = \frac{V^2}{R} = \frac{9^2}{36} = 2.25\,\mathrm{W} (with the switch closed; open switch → no current, no power).
  2. 9 V on 40\,\Omega: the voltage source fixes V, Ohm's law gives I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{9}{40} = 0.225\,\mathrm{A} = 225\,\mathrm{mA}.
  3. 10 mA into 2.2\,\mathrm{k}\Omega: the current source fixes I, Ohm's law gives V = IR = 0.01 \cdot 2200 = 22\,\mathrm{V}.

The pattern: a voltage source fixes V and the load decides I; a current source fixes I and the load decides V.

Resistors in series

For one block, R = \frac{\rho l}{A}. Two blocks of the same cross-section placed end to end:

R = \frac{\rho (l_1 + l_2)}{A} = \frac{\rho l_1}{A} + \frac{\rho l_2}{A} = R_1 + R_2, \qquad R_{\mathrm{Total}} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + \dots + R_N
Symbols
  • l_1, l_2 — lengths of the two blocks (m); \rho, A — resistivity and cross-section, the same for both
  • R_1, R_2, \dots, R_N — the individual resistances in series; N — how many
  • R_{\mathrm{Total}} (also R_T) — the equivalent resistance of the whole chain (Ω)

Example: a string of resistors is placed in series: 120\,\Omega, 390\,\Omega, 560\,\Omega and 470\,\Omega. Equivalent series value:

R_T = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + R_4 = 120\,\Omega + 390\,\Omega + 560\,\Omega + 470\,\Omega = 1540\,\Omega

Sources in series

  • Multiple voltage sources can be connected in series.
  • The equivalent series voltage is the sum of the voltages, considering the polarities.
  • Multiple current sources in series are NOT ALLOWED.
Why are current sources in series forbidden (and voltage sources in parallel)?

In series, the same current must flow through every element. Two ideal current sources each insist on their current, I_1 and I_2; unless I_1 = I_2 exactly, the circuit asks one wire to carry two different currents — a contradiction. The parallel case is the mirror image: elements in parallel share one voltage, so two voltage sources of different value contradict each other (in reality a huge current flows from one into the other). Hence the exception on the slides: equal voltages are fine.

Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL)

  • The sum of voltage rises around a series loop must equal the sum of voltage drops.
  • Voltage rises are due to voltage sources.
  • Voltage drops are due to resistances.

Slide examples:

  • Determine the voltage across the resistors: a 12 V source with 200\,\Omega and 100\,\Omega in series.
  • Determine the voltage V_a across the current source: a 5 A source driving 1\,\Omega, 3\,\Omega and 10\,\Omega in series.
  • Determine the voltage V_{BE} in a single loop with a 24 V, a 6 V and a 4 V source and 10\,\mathrm{k}\Omega, 2\,\mathrm{k}\Omega, 1\,\mathrm{k}\Omega resistors.
Why must the rises equal the drops?

Voltage is energy per charge. Follow one coulomb once around a closed loop: it ends where it started, at the same potential, so it must have lost exactly the energy it gained. Sources lift it (rises), resistors take the energy as heat (drops). Equivalently, the potential at a point is unique — like height on a hiking loop, all ups and downs add to zero.

Worked example — the two KVL loops with a known current
  1. 12 V loop: one loop → one current. R_T = 200 + 100 = 300\,\Omega, so I = \frac{12}{300} = 40\,\mathrm{mA}.
  2. Drops: V_{200} = 0.04 \cdot 200 = 8\,\mathrm{V}, V_{100} = 0.04 \cdot 100 = 4\,\mathrm{V}.
  3. KVL check: 8 + 4 = 12\,\mathrm{V} — drops equal the rise. The larger resistor takes the larger share: this is a voltage divider, V_x = V \frac{R_x}{R_T}.
  4. 5 A loop: the current source fixes I = 5\,\mathrm{A} through 1 + 3 + 10 = 14\,\Omega, so the resistors drop 5 \cdot 14 = 70\,\mathrm{V} in total, and by KVL the source must supply exactly that: \lvert V_a \rvert = 70\,\mathrm{V}. Its sign follows from the arrow: the source pushes current out at the grounded bottom terminal, through 10\,\Omega, 3\,\Omega and 1\,\Omega to a — each resistor drops potential along the flow, so a is the lowest point: V_a = -70\,\mathrm{V}.
Common mistake

Adding source voltages without looking at their polarity. Two sources in the same loop help each other only if, walking around the loop, you pass both from - to +. If you pass one from + to -, it counts as a drop and is subtracted. Mark the + (long plate) of each battery before writing the KVL equation — this decides the V_{BE} example.

Resistors in parallel

Two blocks of the same length placed side by side add their cross-sections:

R = \frac{\rho l}{A_1 + A_2} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{1}{R} = \frac{A_1 + A_2}{\rho l} = \frac{A_1}{\rho l} + \frac{A_2}{\rho l} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}
\frac{1}{R_T} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \dots + \frac{1}{R_N}
Symbols
  • A_1, A_2 — cross-sections of the two side-by-side blocks (m²); l — their common length; \rho — resistivity
  • R_1, \dots, R_N — the individual resistances in parallel; R_T — the equivalent (total) resistance (Ω)

Sources in parallel

  • Current sources can be placed in parallel.
  • The total current is the sum of the currents, considering the polarity.
  • Do not place voltage sources in parallel (exception: when the voltages are the same).

Example: resistors of 2\,\mathrm{k}\Omega, 6\,\mathrm{k}\Omega and 12\,\mathrm{k}\Omega in parallel. Equivalent parallel value:

R_T = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{2\,\mathrm{k}\Omega} + \frac{1}{6\,\mathrm{k}\Omega} + \frac{1}{12\,\mathrm{k}\Omega}} = 1.333\,\mathrm{k}\Omega
Common mistake

Adding parallel resistances like series ones, or forgetting the final inversion (\frac{1}{R_T} = 0.75\,\mathrm{mS} is not R_T). Quick check: the parallel equivalent is always smaller than the smallest resistor — here 1.333\,\mathrm{k}\Omega < 2\,\mathrm{k}\Omega — because every added branch is one more path for the current. Shortcut for two resistors: R_1 \parallel R_2 = \frac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}.

Kirchhoff's current law (KCL)

  • The sum of all currents entering and exiting a node must sum to zero.
  • Example: a source I feeding R_1 and R_2 in parallel: I - I_1 - I_2 = 0, i.e. I = I_1 + I_2.

Example: a simple parallel network — determine the current through each resistor: (1) a 10 A source with 15\,\Omega and 5\,\Omega; (2) 200\,\Omega, 60\,\Omega, 120\,\Omega with a 1 A and a 400 mA source, both pointing up.

Worked example — the two KCL networks
  1. Network 1, common voltage: in parallel all elements share one voltage. R_T = 15 \parallel 5 = 3.75\,\Omega, so V = 10 \cdot 3.75 = 37.5\,\mathrm{V}.
  2. Branch currents: I_{15} = \frac{37.5}{15} = 2.5\,\mathrm{A}, I_5 = \frac{37.5}{5} = 7.5\,\mathrm{A}. KCL check: 2.5 + 7.5 = 10\,\mathrm{A}. Note the smaller resistor takes the larger current (current divider).
  3. Network 2, combine the sources: both point the same way, so 1 + 0.4 = 1.4\,\mathrm{A} in total.
  4. Common voltage: \frac{1}{R_T} = \frac{1}{200} + \frac{1}{60} + \frac{1}{120} = 0.03\,\mathrm{S}, R_T = 33.3\,\Omega, V = 1.4 \cdot 33.3 \approx 46.7\,\mathrm{V}.
  5. Branch currents: I_{200} \approx 0.233\,\mathrm{A}, I_{60} \approx 0.778\,\mathrm{A}, I_{120} \approx 0.389\,\mathrm{A}; together 1.4\,\mathrm{A}.
Why does KCL hold?

Charge is conserved and a wire junction can't store it. Whatever charge arrives at a node per second must leave it per second, otherwise charge would pile up there. "In = out" is the same as "the signed sum is zero".

Series–parallel circuits

Simplification method:

  • Identify subgroups of resistors that are in series or in parallel within themselves.
  • Replace each subgroup with a single equivalent resistance.
  • Repeat until the circuit is reduced to a single resistance, or alternatively to a simple series-only or parallel-only configuration.

Slide figures: (1) 40\,\Omega and 160\,\Omega in series, together in parallel with 80\,\Omega → 80 \parallel 200 \approx 57.1\,\Omega; (2) a ladder a–10–b–30–c with 40 + 200 from b to e and two 100\,\Omega from c.

Examples

  • Determine V_b: (1) a 6 V source with 250\,\Omega in series, then 1\,\mathrm{k}\Omega \parallel 3\,\mathrm{k}\Omega to ground; (2) a 30 V source with 3\,\mathrm{k}\Omega directly across it and the series pair 2\,\mathrm{k}\Omega (top) and 1\,\mathrm{k}\Omega (bottom), b between them.
  • Determine V_{ac} and the voltages across each resistor:
  • Determine V_b, V_c, V_d, the source current I_s, and the current through the 40\,\Omega resistor:
Worked example — the two V_b circuits (voltage dividers)
  1. 6 V circuit, simplify: 1\,\mathrm{k} \parallel 3\,\mathrm{k} = 750\,\Omega, in series with 250\,\Omega.
  2. Divide: V_b = 6 \cdot \frac{750}{250 + 750} = 4.5\,\mathrm{V}.
  3. 30 V circuit: the 3\,\mathrm{k}\Omega sits directly across the source, so it gets 30 V no matter what and doesn't affect the other branch. The 2\,\mathrm{k}/1\,\mathrm{k} branch divides: V_b = 30 \cdot \frac{1}{2 + 1} = 10\,\mathrm{V}.
Worked example — the 16 V circuit, reduce then expand
  1. Reduce from the far end: 100 \parallel 100 = 50\,\Omega; in series with 30\,\Omega → 80\,\Omega. The other branch from b: 40 + 200 = 240\,\Omega. The two branches are in parallel at b: 240 \parallel 80 = 60\,\Omega. Add the 10\,\Omega: R_T = 70\,\Omega.
  2. Source current: I_s = \frac{16}{70} \approx 0.229\,\mathrm{A}.
  3. Expand back — node b: V_b = I_s \cdot 60 \approx 13.71\,\mathrm{V} (or: 16 - 10 \cdot I_s).
  4. Branch b–d: I_{40} = \frac{13.71}{240} \approx 57.1\,\mathrm{mA}, so V_d = 0.0571 \cdot 200 \approx 11.43\,\mathrm{V}.
  5. Branch b–c: I = \frac{13.71}{80} \approx 0.171\,\mathrm{A}, so V_c = 0.171 \cdot 50 \approx 8.57\,\mathrm{V}.
  6. KCL check at b: 0.0571 + 0.1714 = 0.2286\,\mathrm{A} = I_s.
Worked example — V_{ac} with a current source
  1. The 10 mA enters node b through the 1\,\mathrm{k}\Omega (in series with a current source, it changes nothing about the current — only the source's own voltage).
  2. Paths from b to ground: left 7\,\mathrm{k} + 2\,\mathrm{k} = 9\,\mathrm{k}\Omega; right 10\,\mathrm{k} + (12\,\mathrm{k} \parallel 24\,\mathrm{k}) = 10\,\mathrm{k} + 8\,\mathrm{k} = 18\,\mathrm{k}\Omega. In parallel: 9 \parallel 18 = 6\,\mathrm{k}\Omega, so V_b = 10\,\mathrm{mA} \cdot 6\,\mathrm{k}\Omega = 60\,\mathrm{V}.
  3. Split the current: left \frac{60}{9\,\mathrm{k}} \approx 6.67\,\mathrm{mA}, right \frac{60}{18\,\mathrm{k}} \approx 3.33\,\mathrm{mA}.
  4. Node voltages: V_a = 6.67\,\mathrm{mA} \cdot 2\,\mathrm{k} \approx 13.33\,\mathrm{V}, V_c = 3.33\,\mathrm{mA} \cdot 8\,\mathrm{k} \approx 26.67\,\mathrm{V}, so V_{ac} = V_a - V_c \approx -13.33\,\mathrm{V}.
  5. Each resistor: 7\,\mathrm{k}: 46.67 V; 2\,\mathrm{k}: 13.33 V; 10\,\mathrm{k}: 33.33 V; 12\,\mathrm{k} and 24\,\mathrm{k}: 26.67 V each; 1\,\mathrm{k}: 10 V.

Superposition theorem

  • Useful to analyse multi-source series–parallel circuits.
  • Applicable only to linear and bilateral networks.

  • Steps:

    • For every voltage or current source in the original circuit, create a new sub-circuit. The sub-circuits are identical to the original except that all sources other than the one under consideration are set to zero.
    • Label the current directions and voltage polarities on each sub-circuit, as generated by the source under consideration.
    • Solve each sub-circuit for the desired voltages and/or currents with standard series–parallel analysis. Note the voltage polarities and current directions.
    • Add all the contributions from the sub-circuits to get the final values, accounting for current directions and voltage polarities.

Example: determine V_b using superposition for (1) a circuit with a 15 V and a 6 V source (1\,\mathrm{k}\Omega, 5\,\mathrm{k}\Omega, 4\,\mathrm{k}\Omega), and (2) the circuit below.

Common mistake

"Set to zero" means 0 V for a voltage source — replace it with a wire (short) — and 0 A for a current source — remove it (open). Replacing a current source by a wire, or a voltage source by a gap, changes the circuit and gives wrong contributions.

Worked example — superposition for the 12 mA / 3 mA circuit
  1. Only the 12 mA source (3 mA source opened): from a, 100\,\Omega to ground in parallel with 200 + (50 \parallel 400) = 200 + 44.4 = 244.4\,\Omega. Total 100 \parallel 244.4 \approx 70.97\,\Omega, so V_a \approx 0.852\,\mathrm{V}; the 244.4 Ω branch divides it: V_b' = 0.852 \cdot \frac{44.4}{244.4} \approx +154.8\,\mathrm{mV}.
  2. Only the 3 mA source (12 mA source opened): it pulls 3 mA out of node b. Seen from b: 50 \parallel 400 \parallel (200 + 100) = 38.7\,\Omega, so V_b'' = -3\,\mathrm{mA} \cdot 38.7\,\Omega \approx -116.1\,\mathrm{mV}.
  3. Add with signs: V_b = 154.8 - 116.1 \approx 38.7\,\mathrm{mV} (checked against a direct nodal solution of the full circuit).
Why does superposition need a linear network?

Superposition says "the effect of two causes is the sum of their effects". That's true exactly when every element's response is proportional to its input — resistors obey V = IR, so doubling the current doubles the voltage, and two currents through the same resistor give the sum of their voltages. A diode or lamp whose resistance changes with current breaks this. Note that power is not linear even in a resistor (P = I^2 R): you can superpose currents and voltages, then compute power from the totals — never add the powers of the sub-circuits.

Reference

James M. Fiore, DC Electrical Circuit Analysis: A Practical Approach (open textbook): https://open.umn.edu/opentextbooks/textbooks/dc-electrical-circuit-analysis-a-practical-approach-fiore

Connection

Charge, voltage and current in physics terms are in 5 Electromagnetism and Structure of Matter. The circuits here are how sensors become readable: a potentiometer is a voltage divider (2 Sensors), and motor drivers deliver P = VI to the actuators of 3 Actuators. Turning such voltages into numbers is the topic of 9 Measurement and Signal Processing.
